entry.evidence: However, the integrated ME to breed the earthquake is rarely reported to quantitative details.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

steps.action: The authors pose the gap: the mechanical environment (stress, pore-fluid pressure, friction) of faults that breed Mw ≥ 9 megathrust earthquakes is little known in quantitative detail.
steps.quote: We know little about the mechanical environment (ME) of faults to breed them in quantitative details

steps.action: The authors cite the published qualitative explanations of the 60 m shallow slip: dynamic overshoot, or low frictional resistance.
steps.quote: qualitatively explained with dynamic overshoot9 or low frictional resistance of the [...]

steps.action: The authors cite the JFAST borehole results: the breakout stress azimuth, a stress magnitude of about 87 MPa, and laboratory friction values on core samples.
steps.quote: drilled to the ruptured fault at shallow depth and made borehole measurements

steps.action: The authors propose a recovery method that splits the total stress change into effective-stress and pore-pressure changes, closed by Coulomb failure criteria (foreshocks pre-rupture, aftershocks post-rupture) and an undrained Skempton relation.
steps.quote: Here, we propose a method to recover a possible integrate ME in the rupture zone of the Tohoku-Oki earthquake as follows.

steps.action: The authors state the aim: recover the integrated ME of the pre- and post-rupture fault inside the zero-shear-stress-drop contour.
steps.quote: our purpose is to recover the integrated ME of the pre- and post-rupture fault of the Tohoku-Oki earthquake

steps.action: The authors take as input the static coseismic fault stress change that they inverted from coseismic deformation in their earlier work (Xie & Cai 2018).
steps.quote: [...] fault stress change inverted by the coseismic deformation 3 h before and 3 h after the earthquake18

steps.action: The authors solve the stress tensor change by finite elements, then grid-search effective principal stresses, orientations, friction and Skempton B within literature ranges (error threshold 0.01 MPa). They average the admissible solutions by eigen-decomposition, and add lithostatic vertical stress to obtain pore pressures and total stresses.
steps.quote: we recovered the integrated ME (Table S2) in the rupture zone three hours before and three hours after the mainshock

steps.action: The authors compare the recovered values with the JFAST borehole and laboratory values: S1 direction against the breakout average, total intermediate stress (88.9 vs 87 MPa) and its orientation, and fault shear stress (1.1 vs 1.32 MPa, permeable case).
steps.quote: which is close to 87 MPa estimated by the JFAST

steps.action: The authors map the recovered friction coefficient (a belt up to ~0.55, below 0.3 near the trench), Skempton coefficient, pore-pressure drop and pore-pressure ratio. Four low pore-pressure areas coincide with the four high effective-stress regions A–D.
steps.quote: show four abnormally low areas corresponding to four abnormally high areas of the principal effective stresses

steps.action: The authors compare the mean pre-rupture pore-fluid pressure ratio (0.950) with a published force-balance estimate (0.965).
steps.quote: which is close to 0.965 estimated from force balance in a two-dimension model of Japan20

steps.action: The authors check the method's premises: shear stresses predicted from the recovered stresses against the inverted input (<0.1 MPa), the plane sub-fault approximation (<1% loss), and sensitivity to rock properties (<1 MPa for a 6% Vp change).
steps.quote: These uncertainties allow us conclude that the integrated ME recovered is reliable.

steps.action: The authors derive the pre- and post-seismic shear and normal stresses and effective friction coefficients on the fault from the recovered principal effective stresses.
steps.quote: which are determined by the recovered pre- and post-seismic principal effective stresses

steps.action: The authors compare the pre- minus post-seismic mean shear stress (4.5 − (−1.7) MPa) with the inverted mean stress drop of 6.2 MPa. They compare the post-seismic shear with the 2.2 MPa gravity-resisting shear.
steps.quote: The difference of them is right the mean shear stress drop of 6.2 MPa inverted (Fig. 1a) in the rupture area

steps.action: The authors keep shear-stress overshoot as the cause of the unusual stress drop and large shallow slip. They add low trench strength in regions C and D as a reason the rupture reached the trench.
steps.quote: This result quantitatively proves that there exists shear stress overshoot in the rupture area

steps.action: The authors propose that more dilatancy microcracks raise permeability, lowering pore pressure and raising effective stress in regions A–D.
steps.quote: The regions with lower pore-fluid pressure may be explained by that there are more rock microcracks than those of their surroundings.

steps.action: The authors check the microcrack explanation against the higher recovered Skempton coefficient B in those regions.
steps.quote: This explanation is supported by the higher value of Skempton coefficient B in the Fig. 2j

steps.action: The authors compare the post-seismic mean effective friction coefficient (0.029) with the heat-flow-based value of 0.025.
steps.quote: the latter is consistent with 0.025 obtained from modeling heat flow data at the Japan Trench22

steps.action: The authors cite seismic reflection evidence of horst and graben structure on the subducting plate, and the 1896 Sanriku tsunami earthquake in that structure.
steps.quote: show the presence of horst and graben structure on the subducting plate23, 24–25

steps.action: Defining asperity as relatively high frictional strength, the authors keep a large asperity made of two asperities in the pre-rupture ME, with high friction and low pore pressure.
steps.quote: may host a large asperity composed of two asperities

steps.action: The authors suggest, without a further test, that horsts create the asperities and grabens keep near-lithostatic pore pressure, so the horst and graben system bred the earthquake.
steps.quote: It is the horst and graben structure that breed the Tohoku-Oki megathrust earthquake.

end.claim: The recovered integrated mechanical environment of the Tohoku-Oki rupture zone (principal effective stresses with SDs, friction, Skempton coefficient, pore-fluid pressure) contains a large asperity made of two asperities with relatively high friction and relatively low pore-fluid pressure.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the constrained grid-search inversion of the stress-tensor change into pre- and post-rupture effective stresses, friction and pore pressure, no ME, asperity or overshoot claim would exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the input is the authors' 2018 stress inversion; no hypothesis directed new data acquisition (§1 ¶5). Claim: the recovered values could have disagreed with the JFAST, heat-flow and force-balance values (§2 ¶5–¶7, §3 ¶4), but these are point comparisons. The asperity and horst-graben claims face no test they could fail (§3 ¶6). Registration: the search ranges come from the literature (§4.1 ¶9); nothing is said to be fixed before the analysis.

imports.item: finite element solution of the boundary value problem for the coseismic displacement and stress tensor
Skempton coefficient B for undrained pore-pressure change
Coulomb failure criterion closing the underdetermined system

novelty_claims.quote: We discover from this environment a large asperity composed of two asperities induced by relatively high friction coefficients and relatively lower pore-fluid pressures.
Here, we propose a method to recover a possible integrate ME in the rupture zone of the Tohoku-Oki earthquake as follows.
This result quantitatively proves that there exists shear stress overshoot in the rupture area
the integrated ME to breed the earthquake is rarely reported to quantitative details

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: shear-stress overshoot is best_explanation (an arithmetic consistency between derived shear stresses and the inverted stress drop, though the authors say 'proves'); the microcrack/dilatancy explanation of low pore pressure is best_explanation with one supporting line (Skempton B); the horst-graben origin of the asperities is a hypothesis with status none. The document does not show: a synthetic test of whether the grid search recovers a known ME; how the many admissible solutions spread, or what the reported SDs mean (inference: the spread of admissible solutions at each sampling point); sensitivity to the search ranges for friction (0–0.7, 0.85/0.6) and B (0.5–0.9), or to the lithostatic and full-release assumptions. The external checks are point or mean comparisons, mostly at the single JFAST site. The input stress change is the authors' own earlier inversion and is not re-examined. The cited rival explanations are not given distinct predictions. No peer-review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Composition none_fits: a single live event, a new estimation method applied once, and interpretation afterwards; there is no crucial test among rivals, no repeated traces and no exploration phase.

disagreements.target: Qualitative explanations of the large shallow slip by dynamic overshoot (Ide et al. 2011) or low frictional resistance (Lin et al. 2013; Ujiie et al. 2013; Fulton et al. 2013)
disagreements.support: The authors claim a quantitative demonstration of shear-stress overshoot from pre- and post-seismic shear stresses whose difference matches the inverted 6.2 MPa stress drop. They also find low shear strength at the trench.
disagreements.quote: has been qualitatively explained with dynamic overshoot9 or low frictional resistance of the [...]

alternatives_considered.chosen: Average of admissible solutions via the eigenvalue problem of the summed effective stress tensors
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Direct summation of the principal effective stresses
alternatives_considered.reason: The solutions are tensors with different directions and cannot be summed directly
Maximum curvature below 0.005 (nearly a straight line)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Accepted fault geometry and PREM rock properties
alternatives_considered.reason: Geometry constrained by seismic tomography and earthquake distribution; properties widely accepted

alternatives_considered.chosen: Neglect fault cohesion in the Coulomb criterion
alternatives_considered.reason: Cohesion is much less than the principal stresses
